claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.

Rather than using a scalar, the similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj is modeled by a distribution (probabilistic similarity) based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation.

For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node and a graph-based model is employed to jointly infer the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each query-prototype pair.
The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses which exploit the estimated uncertainty.
Few-shot image classification aims to classify query samples of new categories given only a few labeled support samples of these categories as examples.

In few-shot image classification, the feature embeddings of support samples of a category are averaged to form the prototype of that category, and the set of prototypes acts as a similarity-based classifier to identify the category of a query sample by finding the nearest prototype over the support set in the embedding space.

fact_fields.method: prototype averaging of support sample feature embeddings

claim_records.text: During training, for a query sample, the logit vector (classification probability) is obtained by feeding the similarities between the query sample and the prototypes to a SoftMax function.

fact_fields.method: SoftMax function applied to query-prototype similarities

claim_records.text: The reliability of the estimated similarity is vital to the classification performance in few-shot image classification.
Aleatoric uncertainty identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample, capturing the noise inherent in the observations.
For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on the calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs.
An observed similarity of a query-prototype pair, being a one time sampling, suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.
For each few-shot task during optimization, the number of experienced query-prototype pairs is limited, and the side effect of observation noises due to high uncertainty limits the optimization.

For each query-prototype pair, the observed feature similarity between the query and the prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of this distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.

fact_fields.method: conversion of observed feature similarity from scalar to distribution

claim_records.text: The similarity-based classification losses are calculated based on the converted probabilistic similarity representations.

claim_records.text: Existing metric-based few-shot classification algorithms often fail to generalize to unseen domains due to large discrepancy of feature distribution across domains.

The core idea of the proposed method is to use feature-wise transformation layers for augmenting image features using affine transforms to simulate various feature distributions under different domains in the training stage.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers with affine transforms

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of feature distributions under different domains.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies are conducted under the domain generalization setting using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models and provides consistent improvements on few-shot classification performance under domain shift.
Metric-based few-shot classification methods consist of a feature encoder and a metric function, making predictions based on the similarity between query images and support examples.
The feature encoder first extracts image features, and the metric function takes features of both labeled and unlabeled images as input to predict the category of query images.
Existing metric-based approaches do not generalize well to categories from different domains.
The distributions of image features extracted from tasks in unseen domains are significantly different from those in seen domains.
Unsupervised domain adaptation approaches assume that numerous unlabeled images are available in the target domain during training.
Domain generalization methods learn classifiers that generalize well to multiple unseen domains without requiring access to data from those domains.
During training, the metric function may overfit to feature distributions encoded only from seen domains and thus fail to generalize to unseen domains.

Feature-wise transformation layers integrated into the feature encoder modulate feature activations with affine transformations to simulate various distributions of image features during training, improving the generalization ability of the metric function in the testing phase.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers integrated into feature encoder

claim_records.text: The hyper-parameters of feature-wise transformation layers may require meticulous hand-tuning due to the difficulty to model complex variation of image feature distributions across various domains.
A learning-to-learn algorithm is developed to optimize the proposed feature-wise transformation layers so that the model can work well on unseen domains after training using seen domains.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layers are method-agnostic and can be applied to various metric-based few-shot classification approaches for improving their generalization to unseen domains.

claim_records.text: The Relation Network (RN) is trained end-to-end from scratch for few-shot learning.
During meta-learning, RN learns a deep distance metric to compare images within episodes designed to simulate the few-shot setting.
Once trained, RN classifies images of new classes by computing relation scores between query images and few examples of each new class without further network updates.
The RN framework is easily extended to zero-shot learning in addition to few-shot learning.
Extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate the RN approach provides a unified and effective method for both few-shot and zero-shot learning tasks.
RN provides improved performance on few-shot learning compared to prior approaches.

claim_records.text: Existing CLIP-based few-shot classification approaches such as CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features fully aligned with textual features representing the summary of an image.
Local representations (LRs) at low-level are more consistent between seen and unseen samples than high-level representations for few-shot classification.
The proposed MF-Adapter combines complementary strengths of low-level local representations and high-level semantic representations for few-shot classification.
The Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric that measures category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.
Extensive experiments show MF-Adapter outperforms state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, with stronger performance on challenging visual classification tasks.

claim_records.text: Prototypical networks are proposed for few-shot classification, where a classifier must generalize to new classes not seen in the training set given only a small number of examples of each new class.
Prototypical networks learn a metric space in which classification can be performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class.
Compared to recent approaches for few-shot learning, prototypical networks reflect a simpler inductive bias that is beneficial in the limited-data regime and achieve excellent results.
An analysis shows that some simple design decisions can yield substantial improvements over recent approaches involving complicated architectural choices and meta-learning.

claim_records.text: The subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image by exploiting a subspace in local CNN feature space, and measures similarity between two images according to a weighted subspace distance (WSD).

When K images are available for each class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image, in contrast to most previous works that adopted global vector representation.

Experiments on three public benchmark datasets (MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB)) illustrate competitive/superior performance of the SRL method compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

claim_records.text: The core idea of metric-based few-shot image classification is to directly measure the relations between query images and support classes to learn transferable feature embeddings.
Previous work mainly focusing on image-level feature representations cannot effectively estimate a class's distribution due to the scarcity of samples.
Some recent work shows that local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.
Existing local descriptor based works are still based on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure the relations between query images and support classes.
Given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class, an asymmetric measure is more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning.
The Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network for few-shot learning calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

The Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network for few-shot learning calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
RankDNN's core component is a simple MLP that takes an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN effectively improves the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.

claim_records.text: DeepEMD employs the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) as a metric to compute a structural distance between dense image representations to determine image relevance.
The EMD generates optimal matching flows between structural elements that have the minimum matching cost, which is used to calculate the image distance for classification.

DeepEMD designs a cross-reference mechanism to generate important weights of elements in the EMD formulation, which can effectively alleviate the adverse impact caused by cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations.
To implement k-shot classification, DeepEMD proposes to learn a structured fully connected layer that can directly classify dense image representations with the EMD.
Based on the implicit function theorem, the EMD can be inserted as a layer into the network for end-to-end training.

DeepEMD outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin on five widely used few-shot classification benchmarks: miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Fewshot-CIFAR100 (FC100), Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB), and CIFAR-FewShot (CIFAR-FS).
DeepEMD demonstrates effectiveness on the image retrieval task in its experiments.

claim_records.text: The proposed QSFormer model involves a global query-support sample Transformer (sampleFormer) branch and a local patch Transformer (patchFormer) learning branch.
The sampleFormer branch adopts Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model Support representation, Query image representation and metric learning for the few-shot classification task.

The local patch Transformer extracts structural representation for each image sample by capturing the long-range dependence of local image patches, serving as a complement to the global learning branch.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as an effective backbone module for the few-shot learning method.
All modules of the QSFormer framework are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, thereby overlooking the contribution of shallow features.
The proposed approach utilizes a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into distinct feature spaces.
The proposed method extracts feature vectors at different stages, enabling the model to capture both global and abstract features.
Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.
Cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets were performed, achieving high accuracy in the testing domains.
The evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in comparison to state-of-the-art approaches.

claim_records.text: Few-shot image classification aims to recognize novel classes given few labeled images from base classes.
Recent metric-learning few-shot image classification methods typically use a measure at only the image feature level.

fact_fields.method: recent metric-learning few-shot image classification methods

claim_records.text: Measuring similarity only at the image feature level may not be effective enough to generalize from base to novel classes when using only a few images.
The proposed multi-level correlation network (MLCN) for few-shot image classification tackles the limited generalization problem by effectively capturing local information.
MLCN presents a self-correlation module and cross-correlation module to learn the semantic correspondence relation of local information based on learned representations.
MLCN proposes a pattern-correlation module to capture the pattern of fine-grained images and find relevant structural patterns between base classes and novel classes.
Extensive experiments and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed MLCN method on four widely-used few-shot image classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: The optimized empirical criterion of the proposed approach associates two types of sub-task constraints: metric discriminating capacity and accurate attribute prediction.

The proposed zero-shot learning formulation does not require the notion of class in the training phase, with only pairs of image/attributes augmented with a consistency indicator given as ground truth.
At test time, the learned model can predict the consistency of a test image with a given set of attributes, allowing flexible ways to produce recognition inferences.
The proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art results on four challenging datasets used for zero-shot recognition evaluation.

claims: The proposed zero-shot image classification approach controls semantic embedding of images by formulating it as a metric learning problem.
The optimized empirical criterion of the proposed approach associates two types of sub-task constraints: metric discriminating capacity and accurate attribute prediction.

The proposed zero-shot learning formulation does not require the notion of class in the training phase, with only pairs of image/attributes augmented with a consistency indicator given as ground truth.
At test time, the learned model can predict the consistency of a test image with a given set of attributes, allowing flexible ways to produce recognition inferences.
The proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art results on four challenging datasets used for zero-shot recognition evaluation.

ProtoTransfer outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on few-shot tasks from the mini-ImageNet dataset.
In few-shot experiments with domain shift, ProtoTransfer has comparable performance to supervised methods but requires orders of magnitude fewer labels.

claim_records.text: FewSAR is a novel few-shot SAR image classification benchmark consisting of an open-source Python code library of 15 classic methods in three categories for few-shot SAR image classification.
Within the FewSAR benchmark, metric learning methods achieve the best accuracy results on few-shot SAR images under the same setting.
Meta-learning methods and fine-tuning methods perform poorly on few-shot SAR images within the FewSAR benchmark, primarily due to the bias of existing datasets.

The lack of a unified benchmark for SAR target image classification is a key reason for slower progress compared to visible light dataset development, leading to inefficient result comparison and impeded progress.
FewSAR provides an accessible and customizable testbed for different few-shot SAR image classification tasks.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks built on the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized using pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
STN applies the Euclidean distance measure to extracted global features and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to extracted local features.
STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization, then weighting the normalized results to produce the final similarity score.
During the training phase, STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.
STN achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: The proposed Multi-Space Prototypical Learning (MSPL) framework for few-shot attack detection integrates Euclidean, Cosine, Chebyshev, and Wasserstein distances via a constrained weighting scheme to enhance embedding robustness and improve pattern recognition.
MSPL leverages Polyak-averaged prototype generation to stabilize the learning process and effectively adapt to rare and zero-day attacks.
MSPL uses an episodic training paradigm to ensure balanced representation across diverse attack classes, enabling robust generalization.
Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that MSPL outperforms traditional approaches in detecting low-profile and novel attack types.
MSPL is established as a robust solution for zero-day attack detection based on benchmark dataset experimental results.

claim_records.text: Under a strictly matched iso-episode-budget protocol (250 meta-training episodes, 5 canonical seeds, 600 evaluation episodes per seed), the architecture achieves consistent 5-shot accuracy gains across all five seeds over Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML on both CIFAR-FS and MiniImageNet.
The architecture uses 27-53% fewer parameters than any of the compared baselines (Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, MAML) under the matched iso-episode-budget protocol.

The architecture generalizes better to the unseen fine-grained CUB-200-2011 birds domain with zero retraining than the compared baselines.
The architecture is more robust to 50% occlusion and 25% spatial translation than all three compared baselines (Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, MAML).

Falsification ablations (zeroing relational tokens at inference and retraining without them entirely) show the architecture's pairwise relational computation is not the primary driver of its performance; the content-adaptive patch locator is.

MCL is related to learning a centrality on an affiliation network and can be plugged into existing methods by highlighting centralized local features.

claim_records.text: The proposed model consists of a feature generator that can generate various visual features given class embeddings as input.
The proposed model includes a regressor that maps each visual feature back to its corresponding class embedding.
The proposed model includes a discriminator that learns to evaluate the closeness of an image feature and a class embedding.
All three components of the proposed model are trained under the combination of cyclic consistency loss and dual adversarial loss.
The proposed model provides a unified framework for three different approaches: visual->semantic mapping, semantic->visual mapping, and metric learning.
Experimental results show that the proposed model preserves higher accuracy in classifying images from seen classes.
Experimental results show that the proposed model performs better than existing state-of-the-art models in classifying images from unseen classes.

claim_records.text: Existing cache-based adaptation approaches such as Tip-Adapter inherit CLIP's tendency to encode global, general-purpose representations that are not optimally discriminative for adapting generalist models to specialist domains in low-data regimes.

The proposed relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

fact_fields.method: Residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits

claim_records.text: Extensive evaluations on 11 benchmarks show consistent gains over state-of-the-art CLIP adapter and cache-based baselines while preserving zero-shot efficiency.

fact_fields.method: Patch-driven relational gated graph attention cache adaptation

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two steps: 1) Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and 2) Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The Relation Mining Process (RMP) of HelixFormer enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, to achieve better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

The Representation Enhancement Process (REP) of HelixFormer uses CSRMs to strengthen extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.
Extensive experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks show that HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: Image background common in realistic images is empirically identified as a shortcut knowledge helpful for in-class classification but ungeneralizable beyond training categories in Few-Shot Learning.
The COSOC framework is designed to tackle the background shortcut learning problem in FSL by extracting foreground objects in images at both training and evaluation without any extra supervision.
Extensive experiments carried on inductive FSL tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the COSOC approach.
